meta.label: Self-hosting platforms
meta.attribution: Built from software licence files read in each project's own repository, official documentation, security-advisory and pricing pages, not from review sites; CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue is linked as context where a vendor appears in it. Openness reflects whether the licence lets anyone run, modify and redistribute the software without asking permission, not whether a project markets itself as open source; several platforms here are source-available, which restricts commercial use or resale even though the code is public. Accessibility covers both installability and the hardware a person of ordinary skill actually needs, as each project documents it. Transparency reflects whether update and security practice is visible in public, such as a published advisory process or security policy, not whether the software is trustworthy. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: TrueNAS SCALE
products.description: A Debian-based NAS and app platform built on ZFS, with an open source core and separately licensed enterprise extensions.

openness.note: TrueNAS SCALE's end user agreement says the software 'is made available as Open Source Software' but also 'includes Open Source components and some proprietary extensions which are available through additional licences,' naming the TrueNAS Enterprise feature set as an example users may not unlock without a licence.

accessibility.note: TrueNAS SCALE's hardware guide sets a baseline of an x86_64 processor, 8 GB of memory, a 20 GB SSD boot device, and at least two identically sized drives to form a single storage pool.

transparency.note: iXsystems runs a dedicated security-advisories site that rates each reported vulnerability's impact on TrueNAS products and lets researchers file a disclosure by email or Jira ticket; it says it does not currently pay bug bounties.

longevity.note: TrueNAS documents importing a ZFS pool that was exported and disconnected from a system, created on another system, or reconnected after reinstalling TrueNAS, through the web UI or API.

products.name: Proxmox VE
products.description: A Debian-based virtualization platform for running virtual machines and containers, free to use in full without a subscription.

openness.note: Proxmox's own FAQ states plainly: 'Proxmox VE code is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3.'

accessibility.note: The system requirements page lists a bare minimum of 1 GB RAM plus more for guest systems, a 64-bit x86 or ARM CPU with virtualization support, one network card and a hard drive, and says this minimum is for evaluation only, not production use.

transparency.note: Proxmox's security reporting page describes emailing security@proxmox.com, confirming receipt within one Austrian business day, and publishing past and future advisories on a public forum; it does not currently offer paid bug bounties.

economical.note: Proxmox VE's pricing page says every feature, including high availability, live migration, clustering, backup and software-defined storage, is available at every level including none, and that paid subscriptions add only support tickets and access to the enterprise package repository.

products.name: YunoHost
products.description: A Debian-based server operating system built to make self-hosting approachable for people without a systems-administration background.

openness.note: The repository's licence badge and LICENSE file mark YunoHost under the GNU AGPL v3.

accessibility.note: YunoHost's install guide lists seven target hardware paths, including 'an old desktop computer or laptop, or any x86 machine,' a Raspberry Pi, other ARM boards, and rented VPS or dedicated servers.

transparency.note: YunoHost's security page says to contact its security team to discuss flaws, but sets out no published disclosure timeline or advisory database, and tells users to watch the forum and its Mastodon account for word of fixes.

products.name: Umbrel (umbrelOS)
products.description: A home-server OS and app store built first for Umbrel's own hardware, released under a noncommercial source-available licence.

openness.note: The main Umbrel repository is licensed under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0; its README says it is 'free to use, fork, modify, and redistribute Umbrel for personal and nonprofit use' and that commercial use needs a separate agreement with the Umbrel team. A companion repository that builds the OS image, umbrel-os, is separately licensed BSD-3-Clause.

accessibility.note: Umbrel's README says umbrelOS is built first for its own Umbrel Home and Umbrel Pro hardware, and is 'freely available' for Raspberry Pi 5, x86 systems and Linux VMs, where core functionality works on a 'best-effort' basis because of hardware variation.

transparency.note: GitHub reports that Umbrel's main repository has not set up a SECURITY.md file. The separate umbrel-os repository's release history shows infrequent updates: a patch on 17 October 2025 fixing an App Store loading bug, following a release on 22 June 2025.

economical.note: Running umbrelOS on your own hardware costs nothing beyond that hardware, but Umbrel's own device, the Umbrel Home, starts at $549 (or $137.25 a month for four months) for a unit with 512 GB to 4 TB of storage.

products.name: CasaOS
products.description: A lightweight, Apache-licensed personal cloud OS designed to run on general-purpose and single-board hardware.

openness.note: The repository's licence badge and LICENSE file mark CasaOS under Apache-2.0.

accessibility.note: CasaOS's README lists official support for Debian 12, Ubuntu Server 20.04 and Raspberry Pi OS, community support for several more systems, and names ZimaBoard, Intel NUC, Raspberry Pi and general-purpose computers as compatible devices, installed with a single command.

transparency.note: CasaOS's security policy gives an email contact for reporting vulnerabilities and notes the project remains in active development with limited support until it reaches version 1.0.

products.name: OpenMediaVault
products.description: A GPL-licensed, Debian-based network-attached storage platform that has been maintained since 2009.

openness.note: The repository's licence badge and LICENSE-GPL3 file mark OpenMediaVault under GPL-3.0.

accessibility.note: The README describes OpenMediaVault as 'the next generation network attached storage (NAS) solution based on Debian Linux' aimed at home and small-office use, with SSH, FTP, SMB/CIFS and rsync built in and a plugin system for more.

transparency.note: OpenMediaVault's security policy names a security@openmediavault.org contact, asks reporters to withhold public disclosure until a fix and security release are published, and lists what it treats as out of scope, including issues only exploitable by an already-trusted administrator.

products.name: Unraid
products.description: A paid, proprietary NAS, Docker and virtual-machine platform bought as a one-time perpetual licence rather than downloaded free.

openness.note: Unraid is not released under an open-source licence; its purchase page describes only paid Starter, Unleashed or Lifetime licences, with no free or source-available tier.

accessibility.note: Unraid's own docs describe it as an embedded OS that 'can run on nearly any 64-bit x86_64 system while maintaining a minimal memory footprint,' installed by writing it to a USB flash drive that the server then boots from.

transparency.note: Unraid's blog lists dated releases; the most recent at the time of research, 7.2.8 on 29 July 2026, is described as 'a stable, security-focused update' bringing Linux kernel and base-distro package upgrades.

economical.note: Unraid is a one-time purchase, not a subscription: Starter is $49 for up to 6 storage devices, Unleashed is $109 for unlimited devices, and Lifetime is $249 for unlimited devices with updates for life; the first two tiers include only one year of updates.

longevity.note: Unraid's docs say array disks default to XFS, with EXT4, ZFS and BTRFS also selectable, that 'Linux systems can read these file systems natively' while Windows and macOS need extra software, and that a single drive 'acts as a self-contained file system, making data recovery straightforward on any Linux system.'

products.name: Cloudron
products.description: A managed self-hosting platform whose app packages are open source while the core platform is source-available under a paid subscription model.

openness.note: Cloudron's own open-source page describes the platform's code as 'source available,' distinct from open source, while saying 'all Cloudron app packages are open source' on its own GitLab instance.

transparency.note: Cloudron's blog publishes dated posts covering both releases and security topics, for example a security-focused post on SSH authentication logging on 10 August.

economical.note: Cloudron's pricing page offers a free tier limited to two apps, with Pro and Max paid tiers unlocking unlimited apps.

products.name: Synology DSM
products.description: The proprietary operating system bundled with every Synology NAS, the mainstream easy floor most self-hosters compare against.

openness.note: Synology describes DSM as 'the intuitive operating system that powers every Synology NAS,' a proprietary system bundled with its own hardware rather than software installed on a machine you already own.

accessibility.note: Unlike every other option here, DSM ships preinstalled on the NAS unit a buyer purchases, so there is no separate operating-system install step.

transparency.note: Synology's security advisory page lists dated, rated advisories, for example Synology-SA-26:07 DSM, but states it does not publicly announce a vulnerability until a fix is available, nor release exact details before then.

longevity.note: Synology's own migration page says 'Drive migration only works with compatible NAS models or a refreshed version of the same model,' so moving a populated array onto non-Synology hardware is not the documented path; its Migration Assistant instead copies data to a new Synology device.

products.name: CapRover
products.description: A Docker Swarm and nginx-based PaaS for deploying your own apps and databases to a VPS without hand-writing server config.

openness.note: CapRover's LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 with an appendix: paid features 'cannot be modified' or redistributed without a written agreement, while 'any modifications of free features of CapRover should be distributed as free & opensource software.'

accessibility.note: CapRover's getting-started guide says 512MB of RAM 'might not be enough' because the build process is memory-hungry, recommends at least 1GB, and notes most providers sell a 1GB VPS for about $5 a month; it is tested on Ubuntu 24.04 with Docker 25 or newer.

transparency.note: CapRover's security policy asks that vulnerabilities be emailed rather than posted publicly, and says only the most recent release receives security patches.

products.name: Portainer Community Edition
products.description: A permissively licensed management UI for a Docker, Swarm or Kubernetes setup you already have, not a full home-server OS on its own.

openness.note: Portainer's README states the Community Edition uses the zlib licence, and describes Business Edition as building 'on the open-source base' with added features such as role-based access control and support.

accessibility.note: Portainer manages an existing container setup rather than providing one: its README describes it as a platform to 'manage Docker, Swarm, Kubernetes and ACI environments,' which assumes a container runtime is already installed.

transparency.note: Portainer's security policy directs researchers to report privately through GitHub or email, asks that public issues not be used for vulnerabilities, and says it does not run a paid bug bounty programme.

economical.note: Portainer's pricing page says Business Edition is 'free forever for up to 3 nodes' with full features, and separately lists a Home & Student plan at $155 a year for non-commercial use covering up to 15 nodes.

products.name: Runtipi
products.description: A GPL-licensed personal homeserver orchestrator built around a Docker app store on a single Linux box.

openness.note: Runtipi's README states it is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0: 'You may copy, distribute and modify the software as long as you track changes/dates in source files.'

accessibility.note: Runtipi's quick-start guide asks for a 64-bit Linux server, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer recommended, or a Raspberry Pi, with a minimum of 4GB RAM and 10GB of free disk space.

transparency.note: GitHub shows Runtipi has not set up a SECURITY.md file; reports go through GitHub's generic private vulnerability-advisory form instead.

products.name: Cosmos Cloud
products.description: An all-in-one home-server gateway combining a reverse proxy, authentication, container management and an app store, source-available under a no-resale clause.

openness.note: Cosmos Server's README says it is under 'Apache 2.0 Licence with the Commons Clause 1.0': free to use, fork and redistribute, but 'not allowed to sell it, a derivative or to sell a service based on it (ex. SaaS or PaaS).'

accessibility.note: Cosmos's own description bundles a reverse proxy, a multi-factor authentication server, container management, an app store, VPN access, backups, monitoring and identity-provider functions into one system, more to configure than a single-purpose dashboard.

transparency.note: GitHub shows Cosmos-Server has not set up a SECURITY.md file; it relies on GitHub's generic private vulnerability-advisory form.

products.name: PikaPods
products.description: Paid managed hosting of open-source apps: someone else runs the software on infrastructure you rent, and PikaPods says you can take your data and leave.

openness.note: PikaPods hosts existing open-source applications for you rather than being software you run yourself; it says you can 'download your data anytime via SFTP. Move to another host if you prefer.'

accessibility.note: There is no install step: PikaPods is pay-as-you-go from $1.80 a month, scaling with the CPU, memory and storage a pod uses, with $5 of credit given to new accounts.

economical.note: Pricing starts at $1.80 a month and scales with the resources a pod uses rather than a flat per-app fee.

longevity.note: PikaPods says data can be downloaded any time over SFTP and moved to another host, and that backups can be configured to a user's own storage, describing itself as combining 'the privacy of running your own server with the convenience of commercial cloud services.'

products.name: Disroot
products.description: A volunteer-run, donation-funded collective offering a free account across a dozen federated and self-hosted-style FOSS services, the community route rather than a company or a platform you install.

openness.note: Disroot describes its platform as running on '100% free and open source software' across roughly a dozen services, including Nextcloud-based cloud storage, CryptPad, XMPP messaging and Forgejo code hosting.

accessibility.note: Disroot's own donation page states it 'is run by volunteers and offers all the services free of charge,' requiring only a sign-up rather than any server administration.

economical.note: There is no required payment; Disroot funds itself through donations, saying that if every user gave the cost of one monthly coffee, the collective could run without financial strain.

transparency.note: Disroot's donation page publishes a running monthly donation total and supporter count, and its about page says the project has been maintained by an expanding volunteer core team since it was founded in 2015.

products.name: Renting from Big Tech (e.g. Google One)
products.description: The mainstream floor most people already use: keep everything in a rented consumer cloud account instead of running any server yourself.

openness.note: Google One's plans page describes tiered paid storage subscriptions bundled with Gmail, Drive, Photos and Gemini AI features; there is no source code, licence or self-hosting path on offer, only a subscription.

accessibility.note: Every Google account already includes 15 GB of storage at no cost, and paid tiers add capacity starting at $1.99 a month for 100 GB, with nothing to install.

economical.note: Storage is rented indefinitely rather than owned: $1.99 a month for 100 GB, $9.99 for 2 TB, $19.99 for 5 TB, with up to 16% off for paying annually, against a one-time hardware cost for the self-hosted options in this list.

longevity.note: Google's support page for Takeout says a user can export email, documents, calendar, photos, YouTube videos and account activity, but warns that downloading an archive 'doesn't delete it from Google's servers,' and that the download link expires after about 7 days and 5 downloads.

products.name: Nextcloud (All-in-One)
products.description: The most widely known self-hosted file-sync and collaboration suite, installed here through its official All-in-One Docker setup that bundles the server, database, backups and updates.

openness.note: Nextcloud server's COPYING file is the GNU Affero General Public License version 3, and the official All-in-One installer repository carries the same licence.

accessibility.note: The All-in-One README offers a 'Simple web interface included that enables easy installation and maintenance', started from a single Docker container, on x86_64 or arm64 hardware. Getting a valid certificate on the admin interface still needs ports 80 and 8443 reachable and a domain pointing at the server, or a reverse proxy you set up yourself.

longevity.note: The same README says daily BorgBackup backups can be enabled from the interface, to a local path or a remote borg repository, and that an instance can be restored from a backup archive '(you only need the archive and the password in order to restore the whole instance on a new AIO instance)'.

transparency.note: Nextcloud's security page publishes its security advisories and an official CVE database, sets out responsible-disclosure guidelines, and takes vulnerability reports through a public HackerOne programme.

economical.note: Nextcloud's pricing page sells only Enterprise subscriptions, from 100 users at €71.29 per user per year for Standard, and states the product is fully open source under the AGPL. A household can therefore run the same server code without buying a plan.

products.name: Home Assistant OS
products.description: The home-automation platform's own minimal operating system, flashed onto a Raspberry Pi, a mini PC or a virtual machine, or bought preinstalled on the Home Assistant Green; it is a project of a non-profit foundation.

openness.note: The LICENSE file in the Home Assistant Operating System repository is the Apache License 2.0, a permissive licence. Home Assistant itself is also Apache 2.0.

accessibility.note: Home Assistant's installation page offers the Home Assistant Green with the operating system already installed ('No assembly or flashing required.'), or flashing the OS onto a Raspberry Pi, an Odroid or an x86-64 machine you already own. It calls Home Assistant OS the recommended installation type for most people.

transparency.note: Home Assistant's security page asks for vulnerabilities to be reported through GitHub's private Security Advisory system. It asks reporters to give the project 'at least 90 days to release a fixed version' before going public, aims to respond within 7 days, and lists security issues it has handled in the past.

longevity.note: Home Assistant's backup documentation says to back up regularly so that you can restore a system or migrate to new hardware. Backups are encrypted, can run automatically on a schedule, can be stored on network storage, and can be downloaded. A full backup covers the config, share, add-on, SSL and media directories.

economical.note: Home Assistant's Green page lists the ready-made box at a recommended $199 or €179, well below Umbrel's own device here. The operating system itself costs nothing when flashed onto hardware you already own.

products.name: Coolify
products.description: An open-source, self-hostable alternative to Heroku, Netlify and Vercel for deploying apps, databases and one-click services to your own servers over SSH.

openness.note: Coolify's LICENSE file is the Apache License 2.0, and its README describes it as 'Open source & free forever'.

accessibility.note: Coolify's installation docs say it 'needs 2 CPU cores, 2 GB RAM, and 10 GB disk space to run', installed with a one-line script on a supported Linux server. They add that it can run on 1 CPU core and 512 MB RAM, but this is not recommended.

transparency.note: Coolify's security policy says only the 4.x line receives security updates, earlier versions are end of life, and vulnerabilities should be emailed to security@coollabs.io rather than disclosed publicly.

economical.note: Coolify's pricing page says the self-hosted edition is free forever: 'Deploy Coolify on your infrastructure without any restrictions on features.' Only the optional Coolify Cloud control plane, which still runs on servers you bring, is paid.

products.name: Dokku
products.description: A long-running, command-line, Docker-powered 'mini-Heroku' for deploying apps to a single server you control with git push.

openness.note: Dokku's LICENSE file is the MIT licence, granting permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell copies of the software.

accessibility.note: Dokku's installation docs require a fresh Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 or 26.04 or Debian 11+ server on amd64 or arm64, with '1GB of system memory, or add swap memory' for the Docker scheduler, and a domain name recommended. Setup and deploys are driven from the command line; a web dashboard is sold separately as Dokku Pro.

economical.note: Dokku itself is free. Its optional web dashboard, Dokku Pro, is sold as a lifetime licence at $849 covering one production and two pre-production servers, and 'Pro is an add-on to your existing self-hosted Dokku installation', so it is not needed to run apps.

products.name: FreedomBox
products.description: A Debian-based personal server aimed at non-experts, installable on cheap hardware or bought preinstalled, supported by the non-profit FreedomBox Foundation.

openness.note: FreedomBox's COPYING file says the FreedomBox Service (Plinth) is distributed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 or later.

accessibility.note: FreedomBox's homepage says it 'is a private server for non-experts: it lets you install and configure server applications with only a few clicks.' It says it 'runs on cheap hardware of your choice', and offers preinstalled home servers from its hardware partner Olimex.

transparency.note: FreedomBox's manual says it can install security updates automatically, with nightly automatic updates on by default. Stable users mainly get security updates, and a new FreedomBox version is released every two weeks for testing users. There is no dedicated advisory database like TrueNAS's.

longevity.note: FreedomBox's backup manual describes a Borg-based backup of each app's data, configuration and secrets. any remote server reachable over SSH can hold the backup repository, and the backups can be encrypted. It lists gaps: shared-folder data for Samba, Syncthing and similar apps is not included, and backup of user accounts is only planned.

products.name: QNAP QTS
products.description: The proprietary operating system on QNAP NAS units, the main mainstream alternative to Synology; CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue lists 11 QNAP flaws exploited in the wild, 9 of them in ransomware campaigns (2022 to 2023 additions).

openness.note: QNAP's QTS page presents QTS as its NAS operating system, built on a Linux kernel and the ext4 file system. It offers no licence for QTS itself and no way to run it on hardware QNAP did not make. The page renders only with JavaScript and was read in a headless browser.

transparency.note: QNAP's security advisory page lists dated, severity-rated advisories with CVE numbers, for example QSA-26-35, a Critical advisory for QuMagie and License Center dated 8 October 2026. It takes PGP-encrypted reports at security@qnap.com, but says it does not disclose or confirm security issues until patches are available. The list renders only with JavaScript and was read in a headless browser.

products.name: Ubuntu Server + Docker (DIY baseline)
products.description: The do-it-yourself baseline: a general-purpose Linux server with Docker Engine (Apache 2.0) on top, where every app, update and backup is set up by hand rather than through a home-server dashboard.

openness.note: Canonical's intellectual property policy says Ubuntu can be downloaded, used and updated for free and modified for personal or internal use. Each package keeps its own licence, but redistributing a modified Ubuntu under its name needs a licence agreement from Canonical, a trademark restriction the fully open projects here do not carry.

accessibility.note: Ubuntu Server's system requirements give a minimum of 1.5 GB of RAM for ISO installs, a suggested 3 GB or more, and 5 GB of storage, on amd64, arm64 and other architectures. As a general-purpose server OS, it leaves Docker and each service to be installed and maintained from the command line.

transparency.note: Canonical publishes Ubuntu Security Notices as a dated public feed, for example USN-8932-1 for curl and USN-8931-1 for Apache HTTP Server, both on 14 October 2026.

economical.note: Ubuntu is free to download, and Canonical's Ubuntu Pro page says 'Ubuntu Pro is and always will be free for personal use on up to 5 physical machines', which adds extended security maintenance at no cost to a home server.

products.name: Elestio
products.description: Paid managed hosting for more than 400 open-source applications, each on its own dedicated VM at a cloud provider you choose, with root access kept.

openness.note: Elestio hosts existing open-source software for you rather than being software you run yourself; its pricing page offers a search across '400+ open-source software' and a choice of Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS Lightsail, Vultr, Linode, Scaleway or Netcup underneath.

accessibility.note: There is no install step: Elestio's pricing page says 'Every plan includes automated backups, SSL certificates, security updates, OS patches, and 24/7 monitoring', with deployment picked from a catalogue in the browser.

economical.note: Elestio's pricing page says 'Plans start at $11/month for a fully managed service on a dedicated VM'. Each app is billed as its own VM, and paid support tiers cost $50 or $200 a month. That is well above PikaPods' $1.80 starting price for a small app.

longevity.note: The pricing FAQ says that before cancelling 'you can export all your data or download automated backups from the dashboard', and that 'Every service gives you full root access and standard data export options.'
